strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: reducing the substantial inference cost and KV-cache footprint of multimodal language models.

The proposed idea is simple and potentially useful: optimize answer correctness and token retention jointly through post-training, building on an existing dynamic sparse-attention mechanism rather than training a new architecture from scratch.
The empirical coverage is reasonably broad, spanning three Qwen-VL model configurations and 13 image and video benchmarks.
The reported result is promising: token participation falls from roughly 70–80% with ZipVL to 21–24% with ZipR1, while most benchmark scores remain close to the full-attention model.
The manuscript is concise and its central motivation and high-level pipeline are easy to understand.
weaknesses: The central claim of improved inference-time acceleration is not directly evaluated. The paper reports only an average token ratio, with no wall-clock latency, throughput, peak memory, KV-cache size, FLOPs, or hardware-dependent measurements. Token ratio alone does not establish practical speedup because token selection and sparse-kernel overhead can be substantial.

The experimental comparison is inadequate for a top-tier paper. Results include only full attention and the underlying ZipVL method; there are no comparisons with other token-pruning, sparse-attention, or post-training efficiency approaches. Consequently, it is unclear whether ZipR1 is competitive with existing alternatives.

There are no ablations isolating the benefit of reinforcement learning. The paper does not compare against simpler training objectives, accuracy-only or efficiency-only rewards, supervised distillation, rejection sampling, or direct regularization of token retention. It also omits ablations of the KL term, reward weights, threshold sampling strategy, and training data.

The sparse-attention formulation appears technically incorrect as written. In Equation 2, multiplying query and key rows by binary masks before softmax does not restrict attention to selected tokens: masked logits become zero and can still receive nonzero softmax probability, while V is not masked. Masked query rows likewise produce uniform attention rather than being removed. This undermines the mathematical description unless the implementation uses an unstated gather or negative-infinity attention mask.

Important methodological details are missing, including the group size N, learning rate, number of optimization steps, batch size, GRPO clipping and KL coefficients, reward-evaluation procedure, trainable parameters, compute budget, and how response probabilities and KL divergence are computed under changing sparse masks. The work is therefore not reproducible from the paper.

The threshold description is inconsistent: Section 2 states that p is sampled uniformly over [0,1], whereas the experimental setup gives a narrow grid from 0.94 to 0.975. Moreover, the policy probability is written as conditioned only on x rather than on p, leaving the credit-assignment mechanism across different token budgets underspecified.

The equal-weight reward r = r_per + r_eff is insufficiently justified and does not enforce a target accuracy. No Pareto curves are provided across thresholds, so the claimed efficiency-performance tradeoff is supported only at one inference setting. Per-example or per-layer retention distributions are also absent, making the averaged token ratio difficult to interpret.

The reported differences are often small, but there are no repeated runs, confidence intervals, statistical tests, or discussion of evaluation variance. Potential overlap or contamination between the 260k-example training collection and the 13 evaluation benchmarks is not analyzed.

The conceptual novelty is limited: applying standard GRPO with a weighted correctness-plus-efficiency reward to an existing ZipVL policy is straightforward. Stronger technical analysis and substantially more complete evaluation would be needed to elevate this into a top-tier contribution.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: reducing multimodal-LLM prefill computation and KV-cache memory without materially degrading accuracy.
The proposed combination of answer correctness and token reduction in a post-training reward is simple and intuitively aligned with the desired efficiency-quality tradeoff.

weaknesses: The central acceleration claim is unsupported: the paper reports only a token-ratio proxy, with no wall-clock latency, throughput, FLOPs, peak memory, KV-cache size, or sparse-selection overhead measurements on actual hardware.

The formalization of sparse attention appears technically incorrect. Equation 2 zeros rows of Q and K before softmax, but zero logits still receive nonzero probability; this does not restrict attention exclusively to selected tokens as claimed. A proper masked softmax or explicit gathering operation is required.

The token-budget definitions are internally inconsistent. The stated budget counts selected entries in both Q and K and can reach 2ℓ, yet it is divided by ℓ to define a token ratio presented as having a 100% dense maximum. The KV-cache discussion then uses K and V instead. This makes the principal efficiency metric mathematically ambiguous.

The optimization description is underspecified and potentially inconsistent. Responses are generated under different externally sampled thresholds p, but the likelihood ratio is written as π(o|x), without conditioning on p. Moreover, Section 2 samples p from U(0,1), whereas the experimental setup says p is restricted to 0.94–0.975 on a discrete grid.

There are no ablations establishing that RL, the efficiency reward, the accuracy reward, KL regularization, or threshold sampling causes the reported improvement. Comparisons against supervised fine-tuning, distillation, sparsity regularization, or training with randomized thresholds are absent.

The baseline evaluation is inadequate. It compares only full attention and the underlying ZipVL method, omitting other token-pruning and sparse-attention approaches discussed in the literature. There is also no quality-efficiency Pareto curve across inference thresholds, despite flexibility across thresholds being a claimed benefit.

The unusually large change from roughly 70–80% tokens to roughly 22–24% with almost identical accuracy receives no diagnostic validation. The paper provides no variance, repeated runs, confidence intervals, per-task token ratios, qualitative failure analysis, or evidence that evaluation data overlap and contamination from the Video-R1-260k training set were controlled.

Reproducibility is extremely poor: essential details such as the number of GRPO samples, learning rate, batch size, training duration, parameter-update scope, KL and clipping coefficients, reward implementation, correctness grader, dataset splits, compute resources, and code availability are missing.

The novelty is limited to applying a standard GRPO objective with a simple additive correctness-and-sparsity reward on top of ZipVL. The very brief related-work discussion does not convincingly differentiate this approach from alternative post-training, distillation, and sparsity-regularization strategies.

Overall, the manuscript does not provide technically sound definitions or sufficient empirical evidence for its principal claims. The missing system measurements, methodological ambiguities, and absence of ablations are fundamental rather than minor presentation issues.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: reducing the substantial attention and KV-cache costs of high-resolution image and video MLLMs.

The proposed combination of sparse attention and reinforcement-learning post-training is intuitive, deployment-oriented, and potentially useful because it does not require pretraining a new architecture from scratch.

The reported result is striking: across three Qwen2/Qwen2.5-VL models, ZipR1 reduces the average participating-token ratio from roughly 70–80% under ZipVL to about 22–24%, while generally preserving task accuracy.
Evaluation spans 13 established image and video benchmarks and three model configurations, providing encouraging evidence that the effect is not confined to one task or model size.
The method and central reward formulation are presented concisely and are reasonably easy to understand.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not measure actual latency, throughput, FLOPs, peak memory, or KV-cache memory, despite repeatedly claiming inference-time acceleration and relief of computation and memory bottlenecks. Token ratio alone is only a proxy and can substantially overstate wall-clock gains because sparse-selection and irregular-kernel overheads are omitted.

The experimental comparison is too narrow. Only full attention and the underlying ZipVL method are included; there are no comparisons with other training-free or learned visual-token pruning, sparse-attention, or token-merging approaches cited in the paper.

Essential training and reproducibility details are absent, including optimizer and learning rate, number of updates/epochs, batch and GRPO group sizes, values of beta and epsilon, compute budget, trainable parameter scope, decoding settings, and the precise accuracy-reward implementation. No code or resource statement is provided.

There is an internal inconsistency in the sparsity-threshold description: Section 2 states that p is sampled from U(0,1), whereas the experimental setup says p ranges from 0.94 to 0.975 in increments of 0.005. It is unclear which distribution is actually used during training and how the reported inference operating point is selected.

The sparse-attention formulation is technically unclear. Equation 2 masks Q and K before softmax rather than explicitly masking logits or gathering selected tokens; zeroed logits can still receive nonzero softmax probability. The handling of unselected queries and the correspondence between the formalism and the actual ZipVL implementation are not established.

The mechanism by which the proposed GRPO objective actively increases token sparsity needs considerably more justification. The threshold p is externally sampled rather than a policy action, while the likelihood ratio is defined only over generated responses. The paper provides neither derivation nor diagnostic evidence showing that optimization changes attention concentration/token selection rather than merely improving robustness to aggressive pruning.

No ablations isolate the contributions of the efficiency reward, accuracy reward, KL regularization, threshold sampling, or RL itself. A supervised/distillation baseline at matched token ratios is especially important for establishing that GRPO is necessary.

Results are reported as single numbers without uncertainty, repeated runs, statistical tests, per-example trade-off curves, or sensitivity analyses over p and reward weights. Consequently, small claimed accuracy differences cannot be distinguished from evaluation variance.

The use of Video-R1-260k is insufficiently documented, with no discussion of possible overlap or contamination with the 13 evaluation benchmarks. The paper also does not report how image-versus-video training examples contribute to the observed generalization.

The exposition overstates what is demonstrated: token participation is reduced, but actual acceleration is not shown. Terms such as “transfer entropy” are used for ordinary KL regularization without a formal connection, and the paper contains several language and notation issues.

Overall, the central empirical observation is promising, but the missing systems measurements, baselines, ablations, implementation details, and clarification of the optimization mechanism leave the main efficiency and methodological claims insufficiently supported for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: reducing the substantial visual-token and KV-cache costs of multimodal LLM inference.
The proposed combination of multi-budget exploration and joint accuracy-efficiency rewards is intuitive and potentially useful as a post-training approach requiring no new model architecture.

The evaluation is broad, covering four model configurations and thirteen image/video benchmarks. Reported results are promising, with approximately 23–30% token retention while largely preserving dense-model accuracy.
The paper evaluates practical latency and memory, explores multiple sparse-attention mechanisms and budgets, and includes a hallucination-oriented robustness check.
weaknesses: The central mechanism is insufficiently validated. There are no ablations isolating the efficiency reward, correctness reward, group-level indicator, KL term, multi-budget sampling, or RL training itself. Consequently, the experiments do not establish that grouped-rollout RL is necessary or that it causes the gains rather than ordinary fine-tuning on the calibration data.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The paper does not explain how binary correctness is computed for heterogeneous free-form image/video answers, nor report essential training details such as the number of updates or epochs, effective batch size, sampling/decoding settings, optimization schedule, and total training cost. Code and checkpoints are not indicated.

The mathematical presentation contains substantive inconsistencies. Equation 2 zeros queries and keys before softmax, which does not actually remove masked keys because zero logits still receive probability mass. Equation 5 reuses p as both the retention threshold and an integer token count, and the GRPO policy probabilities omit conditioning on the sampled sparsity threshold. The relationship between this objective, discrete top-k selection, and gradients that reshape attention is not rigorously explained.

Baseline comparisons are not sufficiently controlled. Training recipes and compute for the post-training MOBA and sharpness baselines are unspecified, and there is no matched SFT, single-budget training, preference-learning, or correctness-only GRPO baseline. Thus the claimed advantage of the proposed RL formulation remains uncertain.

Efficiency evidence is incomplete. The headline 3.3x speed and 3x memory improvements come from a small runtime study on one model, without sufficient hardware, batch-size, precision, implementation, output-length, or measurement details. The manuscript also alternates between describing the measured latency as prefill, decoding, and overall inference latency.

The training-threshold description is inconsistent: the method states that thresholds are sampled from U(0,1), while the implementation uses the narrow discrete interval [0.94,0.975]. It is also unclear whether different-budget rollouts are otherwise generated with controlled randomness, which affects the interpretation of their relative rewards.

Results lack uncertainty estimates or repeated-run analysis, and no data-overlap or contamination analysis is provided for the large Video-R1-derived calibration set. Some reporting is internally inconsistent, including the Table 3 averages and their differing values in the surrounding text.

Overall, the empirical finding is interesting, but missing causal ablations, incomplete specifications, formulation errors, and under-documented efficiency measurements prevent the evidence from meeting the standard of a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The problem is important: reducing visual-token and KV-cache costs could materially improve long-context multimodal inference.
The method is conceptually simple and compatible with existing pretrained MLLMs and dynamic sparse attention, without requiring training from scratch.
The evaluation covers multiple model sizes and 13 image/video benchmarks. Reported retention near 23–30% with relatively small accuracy loss is promising.
The paper evaluates accuracy-budget curves, latency, memory, attention patterns, robustness, and alternative pruning mechanisms.
weaknesses: The central causal evidence is missing. There is no correctness-only GRPO, comparable SFT/post-training, or efficiency-reward ablation. Consequently, the gains could arise from additional training on 260k examples rather than the proposed sparsity reward or grouped-budget optimization. Most headline comparisons instead pit the post-trained method against training-free baselines.

The mathematical formulation contains substantive errors or ambiguities. Equation 2 does not implement sparse attention: zeroing Q and K before softmax leaves positive probability on supposedly masked positions, while V is unmasked. Equation 5 also overloads p as both the retention threshold and an integer token count. These issues undermine confidence in the technical description.

The RL specification is incomplete. The likelihood in Equation 11 does not condition on the sampled budget threshold, even though it changes the rollout distribution; the answer-level policy-gradient mechanism by which a non-differentiable token-selection process learns greater sparsity is not rigorously derived. Reward computation and correctness judging for the heterogeneous training tasks are also unspecified.

Runtime evidence is insufficient for the strong systems claims. Figure 4 reports only a small number of aggregate curves without hardware, precision, batch size, generation length, kernel details, measurement protocol, or uncertainty. The manuscript variously describes the 3.3x result as prefill latency, inference speed, and decoding speed, although the figure labels it prefill latency.

Token ratio is not a standardized compute measure across methods: pruning at different layers yields different FLOPs, and MInference alone is assigned a FLOPs-equivalent ratio. Thus several efficiency comparisons are not directly comparable.

The evaluation lacks repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, and statistical testing, despite many reported accuracy differences being only a few tenths of a point. There is also no per-category or failure analysis showing where aggressive pruning loses essential evidence.

Several results are internally inconsistent or insufficiently defined. Table 3's unexplained average mixes metrics on incompatible scales, and its values conflict with the surrounding text about whether the full model or Sparsity Forcing scores 70.0, 70.2, or 70.3.

Reproducibility is weak: the paper omits training duration, epochs/steps, effective batch size, sampling and decoding settings, GRPO clipping value, KL implementation, reward parser, checkpoint-selection procedure, sparse-kernel implementation, and training cost. No code or model-release commitment is provided.

The novelty is moderate: the contribution primarily combines an existing sparse-attention method with standard GRPO and a simple correctness-plus-token-reduction reward. Stronger isolation of what grouped RL uniquely contributes is necessary for top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and practically relevant contribution: an inference-aligned RL post-training framework that directly optimizes answer correctness and token retention rather than relying only on attention-sharpness proxies or fixed sparsity patterns.

The empirical results are compelling. Across four MLLM configurations and 13 image/video benchmarks, the method retains only about 23–30% of tokens while generally remaining close to full-attention accuracy and outperforming several training-free and post-training sparsification baselines.

The evaluation has useful breadth, covering different model sizes, model families, modalities, context lengths, and low-budget settings. The HallusionBench experiment also addresses the important concern that aggressive pruning could remove evidence and increase hallucinations.
The paper demonstrates practical systems benefits, reporting up to 3.3x lower latency and 3x lower memory usage, rather than relying exclusively on token-count or FLOP proxies.
The method is conceptually simple, compatible with an existing sparse-attention mechanism, and offers a controllable accuracy-efficiency trade-off at inference time.
weaknesses: The central claim that grouped-rollout RL is necessary or principally responsible for the gains is not adequately isolated. Missing comparisons include supervised fine-tuning of ZipVL at matched budgets, fixed or curriculum-based budget training, and ablations removing either the correctness or efficiency reward.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the paper does not clearly report the number of training steps or epochs, effective batch size, decoding settings, precise correctness-reward implementation for open-ended answers, which parameters are updated, or sufficient details of the sparse kernels and runtime measurement protocol.

No multiple-run results, confidence intervals, or significance tests are provided. Several reported accuracy differences are very small, so it is unclear whether apparent improvements over full attention or competing methods exceed evaluation and training variance.

The systems claims need better-controlled reporting. Hardware, precision, batch size, generated-token count, compilation and kernel details are omitted, and the peak 200k-token latency setting is substantially longer than the approximately 20k-token benchmark context used for LLaVA-Video. Training overhead from sequential multi-budget rollouts is also not quantified.

The formalization of sparse attention is imprecise: zeroing query and key rows in Equation 2 is not generally equivalent to removing tokens from softmax attention, and the relationship between the constrained objective in Equation 3 and the implemented ZipVL selection rule is insufficiently established.

The post-training baseline comparison is narrow and does not establish that all methods received matched data, optimization budgets, and tuning effort. The paper also does not discuss possible overlap between the Video-R1/LLaVA-Video training data and evaluation benchmarks.

Several robustness and mechanism analyses are limited: HallusionBench is shown only as a small plot without exact token ratios or uncertainty, attention-map visualizations are anecdotal, and there is no analysis of which token types or tasks fail under aggressive pruning.
